title: Transitive and intransitive verbs
summary: Self-move verbs move the subject itself; other-move verbs move something else. Many verbs come in pairs, and their endings tell you which is which.

blocks.text: The course replaces the Western labels "intransitive" and "transitive" with **self-move** (自動詞) and **other-move** (他動詞). A **self-move** verb moves the subject itself: the door **opens**, a ball **falls**. An **other-move** verb moves something else: I **open** the door, I **drop** the ball. The two ideas overlap heavily with the Western labels, but self-move / other-move describes what Japanese really does.
The mother and father of all verbs
**ある** (to be, to exist) is the "mother" of every self-move verb: it only looks inward. **する** (to do) is the "father" of every other-move verb: it must do something to something.

items: A verb ending in **-す** is **other-move**: 出す, 落とす, 壊す.
A verb ending in **-ある** (あがる, とまる, はじまる) is **self-move**.
**-める** (止める, 始める) is usually **other-move**, and **-れる / -える** (壊れる, 消える) is usually **self-move**.

blocks.text: These are guides, not laws. Some pairs have to be decided by meaning, but the pairs above cover most everyday verbs.

questions.note: Verbs ending in す are other-move.
A self-move verb has no object: the door is the main carriage.

questions.prompt: （私が）ドア＿＿開ける。 (I open the door.)
questions.note: An other-move verb does something to a thing: を.

questions.note: ある is the purely inward verb; する is the father of other-move verbs.
